proposals.relationship: Lawrence and Miles Taylor criticize Languages of Class for neglecting reception, political contingency and social structure (1993).
proposals.evidence_note: A joint argument by both authors. Their main reply challenges Mayfield and Thorne; it also defends Jones against simple linguistic determinism. Selected primary transcription read, not facsimile-collated; distinct from Lawrence’s 1998 mentoring acknowledgment.
primary_locators: Social History 18.1 (1993), pp. 13–14; opening pp. 1–3 establishes the reply target.

proposals.relationship: Joyce credits Stedman Jones with opening the question of class language but criticizes his formalistic treatment of political language and insufficient attention to its contexts (1991).
proposals.evidence_note: Qualified criticism within an appreciative discussion of alternatives to class and the possibilities of populism. The introduction’s p. 10 was freshly read and visually checked in the publisher’s preview; subsequent chapters and the full book remain unread.
primary_locators: Visions of the People (1991), introduction p. 10, paragraph beginning with the British social historian who opened class language; publisher PDF page 10.

proposals.relationship: Vernon praises Stedman Jones as a catalyst for rethinking English politics while criticizing his privileging of printed texts and neglect of agency, unstable meanings and differences within texts (1993).
proposals.evidence_note: The same paragraph recognizes Jones’s account of politically constitutive language and distinguishes subsequent work by Joyce and Joan Scott. Fresh selected publisher-preview reading, not the whole book; no claim about Vernon’s unread 1994 reply.
primary_locators: Politics and the People (1993), introduction p. 4, paragraph beginning with theoretical reservations about Thompson; publisher PDF page 4.
